lessons.title: The Berlin Wall & the Cuban Missile Crisis

before.content_html:
The Berlin Refugee Problem

By the late 1950s, Berlin had become a flashpoint of Cold War tension. West Berlin was a thriving capitalist outpost deep inside communist East Germany, and it was a constant embarrassment to the Soviet Union. Between 1949 and 1961, around 3 million East Germans fled to the West through Berlin — many of them skilled workers, doctors and engineers whose departure weakened the East German economy. This refugee crisis was humiliating for Khrushchev because it showed that people preferred capitalism to communism.

Khrushchev’s Berlin Ultimatum (1958)

In November 1958, Khrushchev issued an ultimatum to the Western powers: they must leave West Berlin within six months, or he would hand control of all access routes to East Germany. The West refused. A series of summit meetings followed, but none resolved the crisis.

Camp David (1959): Khrushchev and Eisenhower met in a relatively friendly atmosphere. Khrushchev withdrew his ultimatum, but no agreement was reached on Berlin. Paris (1960): The summit collapsed when the USSR shot down an American U-2 spy plane over Soviet territory. Eisenhower refused to apologise, and Khrushchev walked out. Vienna (1961): The new US President Kennedy met Khrushchev. Kennedy was inexperienced and Khrushchev bullied him, reissuing his Berlin ultimatum. Kennedy left shaken, saying it was the “worst thing in my life.”

The Construction of the Berlin Wall (1961)

On 13 August 1961, East German soldiers began sealing the border between East and West Berlin with barbed wire, which was quickly replaced by a concrete wall. The Berlin Wall was heavily guarded with watchtowers, searchlights, minefields and a “death strip” where guards had orders to shoot anyone trying to cross.

Key Fact

The Berlin Wall stopped the flow of refugees almost overnight. It solved the USSR’s refugee problem, but it became the most powerful symbol of the Cold War division of Europe. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross the Wall between 1961 and 1989.

Kennedy protested but did not try to tear the Wall down. He recognised that a wall was preferable to a war. In June 1963, Kennedy visited West Berlin and delivered his famous “Ich bin ein Berliner” speech, declaring American solidarity with the people of West Berlin. The Wall remained in place for 28 years.

The Cuban Revolution & the Bay of Pigs

In 1959, Fidel Castro overthrew the US-backed dictator Batista and took power in Cuba. He nationalised American-owned businesses, which angered the USA. The USA refused to recognise Castro’s government and imposed a trade embargo. Castro turned to the Soviet Union for economic and military support, bringing communism to America’s doorstep — just 90 miles from Florida.

In April 1961, President Kennedy authorised a CIA-backed invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs. Around 1,400 Cuban exiles landed but were quickly defeated by Castro’s forces. The invasion was a humiliating failure that strengthened Castro’s position, pushed Cuba closer to the USSR, and made Kennedy look weak.

The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962)

In October 1962, American U-2 spy planes photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built on Cuba. These missiles could reach most major American cities within minutes. Kennedy faced the most dangerous moment of the entire Cold War.

16 October 1962

Discovery

Kennedy was shown the U-2 photographs. He formed a group of advisers called ExComm to consider the options: a naval blockade, an air strike, an invasion of Cuba, or diplomacy.

22 October 1962

Naval Blockade

Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba on live television, demanding the removal of Soviet missiles. Soviet ships carrying more missiles were sailing towards Cuba.

24–27 October 1962

Brinkmanship

Soviet ships turned back before reaching the blockade line. Khrushchev sent two letters: the first offered to remove missiles if the USA promised not to invade Cuba; the second demanded the USA also remove its missiles from Turkey. On 27 October, a U-2 spy plane was shot down over Cuba, bringing the world to the brink of nuclear war.

28 October 1962

Resolution

Kennedy agreed to Khrushchev’s first letter (no invasion of Cuba) and secretly agreed to remove US missiles from Turkey. Khrushchev agreed to remove Soviet missiles from Cuba. Nuclear war was averted.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days (16–28 October 1962) and was the closest the world came to nuclear war. Kennedy chose the naval blockade as a middle course — strong enough to pressure the USSR but avoiding a direct military attack that could escalate to nuclear conflict.

Kennedy appeared to win: the Soviet missiles were removed from Cuba, and the USA looked strong. However, Kennedy also secretly agreed to remove US missiles from Turkey and promised never to invade Cuba — concessions that were not made public. Khrushchev could claim he had secured Cuba’s safety and forced the removal of US missiles from Turkey, but he was humiliated domestically and was removed from power in 1964 (partly due to this crisis). Castro was furious at being excluded from the negotiations between Kennedy and Khrushchev.

Opposition in Czechoslovakia

By the late 1960s, Czechoslovakia had been under rigid communist control for twenty years. The economy was stagnating, censorship was strict, and the secret police suppressed all dissent. Many Czechs and Slovaks resented Soviet interference and longed for greater freedom. In January 1968, the reformist leader Alexander Dubček was appointed as leader of the Czechoslovak Communist Party.

The Prague Spring (1968)

Dubček introduced a programme of reforms that became known as the Prague Spring. He wanted to create “socialism with a human face” — keeping communism but making it more humane. His reforms included relaxing censorship to allow greater freedom of speech, allowing other political parties to exist alongside the Communist Party, introducing elements of a market economy, and strengthening trade links with the West.

Key Fact

Unlike Nagy in Hungary (1956), Dubček did not try to leave the Warsaw Pact. He wanted to reform communism, not abandon it. Nevertheless, the Soviet Union saw his reforms as a dangerous threat that could spread to other satellite states.

The Soviet leader Brezhnev feared that if Czechoslovakia’s reforms succeeded, other satellite states would demand similar freedoms — a domino effect that could destroy Soviet control of Eastern Europe. East Germany and Poland, whose leaders were hardline communists, pressured Brezhnev to act. The USSR also worried that relaxed censorship would allow anti-Soviet ideas to spread, and that closer trade links with the West would pull Czechoslovakia out of the Soviet economic orbit.

The Soviet Invasion & the Brezhnev Doctrine

On 20–21 August 1968, around 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops from the USSR, Poland, Hungary, East Germany and Bulgaria invaded Czechoslovakia. There was no armed resistance — Dubček ordered his people not to fight, knowing they could not win against overwhelming force. Instead, Czechs and Slovaks used passive resistance: they removed street signs to confuse invading troops, painted anti-Soviet graffiti, and argued with soldiers.

Dubček was arrested, taken to Moscow, and forced to reverse his reforms. He was eventually replaced by the hardliner Gustáv Husák, who restored rigid communist control. Around 100 Czechs and Slovaks were killed during the invasion, and over 300,000 people fled the country.

Key Fact

The Brezhnev Doctrine declared that the USSR had the right to intervene militarily in any socialist country where communism was threatened. It justified the invasion of Czechoslovakia and sent a clear warning to other satellite states: reform would not be tolerated.

International Reaction to the Soviet Invasion

As with Hungary in 1956, the Western response was limited to verbal condemnation. The USA was heavily involved in the Vietnam War and had no appetite for a direct confrontation with the USSR over Czechoslovakia. NATO condemned the invasion but took no military action. The United Nations debated the crisis, but the USSR used its veto to block any resolution.

However, the invasion had wider consequences. Communist parties in Western Europe, particularly in Italy and France, publicly criticised Moscow, weakening Soviet influence in the West. Romania and Yugoslavia refused to take part in the invasion, showing cracks in Soviet control. Albania left the Warsaw Pact entirely in protest.

Consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis

The near-catastrophe of the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 had led both superpowers to take steps to reduce the risk of nuclear war. Several important agreements followed.

1963

The Hotline

A direct communication link (teletype, not a red telephone) was established between the White House and the Kremlin. This meant the leaders could communicate instantly during a crisis, reducing the risk of miscalculation.

1963

Limited Test Ban Treaty

The USA, USSR and Britain agreed to ban nuclear weapons testing in the atmosphere, underwater and in outer space. Underground testing was still allowed. This was the first significant arms control agreement of the Cold War.

1967

Outer Space Treaty

Both superpowers agreed not to place nuclear weapons in space or on the moon. This prevented the arms race from extending beyond Earth.

1968

Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty

The USA, USSR and Britain agreed not to supply nuclear weapons technology to non-nuclear states. This aimed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to more countries.

In June 1963, President Kennedy visited West Berlin and delivered his famous “Ich bin ein Berliner” speech to a crowd of 450,000 people. He declared that the Berlin Wall proved the failure of communism: “Freedom has many difficulties and democracy is not perfect, but we have never had to put a wall up to keep our people in.” The speech was a powerful propaganda statement and a reassurance to West Berliners that the USA would not abandon them. It also had a broader significance — it demonstrated continued American commitment to Western Europe despite the improving relations after Cuba.

before.exam_tip_html: For “Give Two Things” questions (2 marks), keep your answers short and specific. Each inference must be supported by a detail from the source or your own knowledge. For example: “I can infer that the Soviet Union feared losing control of Eastern Europe. I know this because the Brezhnev Doctrine stated the USSR had the right to intervene in any socialist country where communism was threatened.” Don’t write too much — two clear points with supporting detail is all that’s needed.

lessons.title: Détente: SALT, Helsinki & the Limits of Peace

before.exam_tip_html: For “Explain One Cause” questions (4 marks), make sure you identify the cause clearly in your first sentence, then develop it with three further linked points. Use connectives like “this was because,” “which meant that,” and “as a result” to show a chain of reasoning. For example: “One cause of détente was the cost of the arms race. This was because both superpowers were spending huge sums on nuclear weapons, which diverted resources from their economies. As a result, both sides had a financial incentive to agree limits on nuclear weapons, leading to SALT 1 in 1972.”

lessons.title: The Second Cold War: Afghanistan & Reagan’s SDI

before.content_html:
The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan (1979)

In December 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. A communist government had taken power there in 1978, but it faced fierce opposition from Islamic guerrilla fighters known as the mujahideen. When the Afghan government asked for Soviet help, Brezhnev sent over 100,000 troops. He feared that if the communist government fell, it would encourage anti-Soviet movements in the USSR’s own Muslim-majority Central Asian republics.

Key Fact

The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended détente and began what historians call the “Second Cold War.” The war lasted ten years (1979–89), cost over 15,000 Soviet soldiers’ lives, and is often compared to America’s experience in Vietnam — a costly, unwinnable guerrilla war.

The USA saw the invasion as Soviet aggression and expansionism. President Carter’s national security adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski warned that the USSR might be trying to reach the oil-rich Persian Gulf. Whether the invasion was genuinely aggressive or merely defensive (protecting a neighbouring communist government) remains debated by historians.

The Carter Doctrine & Western Response

President Carter responded forcefully to the invasion. In January 1980, he announced the Carter Doctrine, declaring that any attempt by an outside force to gain control of the Persian Gulf region would be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the USA and would be repelled by military force.

Carter also took a series of punitive measures: he withdrew SALT 2 from Senate consideration, imposed a grain embargo on the USSR (cutting off American wheat exports), and increased US defence spending. Most dramatically, the USA boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics, with 64 other nations following suit. The USSR retaliated by boycotting the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

The 1980 Moscow boycott was led by the USA and included 64 other nations, though some major countries like Britain and France allowed their athletes to compete under the Olympic flag rather than their national flags. The boycott embarrassed the Soviet Union but did not change its policy in Afghanistan. In retaliation, the USSR and 13 allies boycotted the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, claiming concerns about “security” for their athletes. The mutual boycotts showed how deeply the Cold War could penetrate even sport.

The USA also began covertly supplying the mujahideen with weapons and money through Pakistan’s intelligence services. This included Stinger anti-aircraft missiles, which proved devastatingly effective against Soviet helicopters. The CIA’s support for the mujahideen was one of the largest covert operations of the Cold War.

Reagan & the “Second Cold War”

In January 1981, Ronald Reagan became US President. He took a far more aggressive stance towards the Soviet Union than Carter had. Reagan believed détente had been a mistake that allowed the USSR to build up its military while the USA relaxed. He called the Soviet Union an “evil empire” and dramatically increased US defence spending — the military budget rose from $178 billion in 1981 to $229 billion by 1985.

Key Fact

Reagan’s strategy was deliberate: he believed the USA could outspend the Soviet Union in an arms race, forcing the USSR to choose between military spending and economic collapse. The Soviet economy, already struggling, could not match American spending.

The Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI / “Star Wars”)

In March 1983, Reagan announced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), nicknamed “Star Wars.” This was a proposed space-based defence system that would use satellites and lasers to shoot down Soviet nuclear missiles before they reached the USA. If it worked, it would make the USA immune to nuclear attack and destroy the principle of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD).

The Soviet Union was alarmed by SDI. If the USA could defend itself against nuclear attack, the USSR’s entire nuclear arsenal would become useless, and the balance of power would shift decisively in America’s favour. Many scientists doubted SDI was technically feasible, and it was never fully built. However, the threat of SDI was enough to worry the Soviet leadership and pressure them into negotiations. SDI became a major obstacle in arms control talks, as the USSR demanded it be abandoned before any new agreements could be reached.

Historians disagree about SDI’s role in ending the Cold War. Some argue that SDI pressured the USSR into negotiations because the Soviet economy could not afford to develop a matching system, ultimately forcing Gorbachev to seek arms reduction deals with the West. Others argue that SDI was never realistic and that the Cold War ended because of the internal weaknesses of the Soviet system and Gorbachev’s own reforms. What is clear is that SDI increased Soviet anxiety and contributed to the sense that the arms race was unsustainable.

lessons.title: Gorbachev & the Collapse of the Soviet Union

before.content_html:
Gorbachev’s “New Thinking”

In March 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Union. At 54, he was much younger than his predecessors and brought a fundamentally different approach to governing. Gorbachev recognised that the Soviet Union was in deep trouble: the economy was stagnating, the war in Afghanistan was draining resources and morale, the arms race was cripplingly expensive, and ordinary Soviet citizens faced shortages of basic goods.

Gorbachev introduced what he called “new thinking” — a willingness to reform the Soviet system and to negotiate with the West rather than confront it. His two signature policies were glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring).

Key Fact

Glasnost meant greater freedom of speech, press freedom and political debate. Perestroika meant reforming the economy by reducing central planning and introducing some market-based elements. Gorbachev wanted to modernise the Soviet system, not destroy it — but his reforms ultimately unleashed forces he could not control.

Reducing Cold War Tensions

Gorbachev and Reagan developed a surprisingly productive relationship. Despite their ideological differences, both leaders recognised the need to reduce the nuclear threat. They held a series of summit meetings that transformed the Cold War.

November 1985

Geneva Summit

Gorbachev and Reagan met for the first time. No major agreements were reached, but the two leaders established a personal rapport and agreed to hold further meetings.

October 1986

Reykjavik Summit

Gorbachev proposed eliminating all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed because Reagan refused to abandon SDI. However, the summit showed both sides were serious about major arms reductions.

December 1987

INF Treaty

Gorbachev and Reagan signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, eliminating all land-based nuclear missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres. This was the first treaty to actually reduce (not just limit) nuclear weapons. Nearly 2,700 missiles were destroyed.

Previous agreements (SALT 1, SALT 2) had only limited the growth of nuclear arsenals. The INF Treaty was the first to require the actual destruction of nuclear weapons — nearly 2,700 missiles were eliminated. It included on-site inspections to verify compliance, demonstrating a level of trust that would have been unthinkable a decade earlier. The treaty removed an entire class of weapons from Europe and showed that genuine disarmament was possible.

Impact on Eastern Europe

Gorbachev’s reforms had a transformative effect on Eastern Europe. He made clear that the Soviet Union would no longer use force to keep communist governments in power — effectively abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine. This was sometimes called the “Sinatra Doctrine” (after Frank Sinatra’s song “My Way”) — satellite states could now go their own way.

Without the threat of Soviet military intervention, opposition movements across Eastern Europe gained momentum. In Poland, the Solidarity trade union movement won free elections in June 1989. In Hungary, the government opened its border with Austria, allowing East Germans to flee west. In Czechoslovakia, the “Velvet Revolution” peacefully removed the communist government. In Romania, the dictator Ceauşescu was overthrown and executed.

The Fall of the Berlin Wall

On 9 November 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened. The East German government, overwhelmed by mass protests and the flood of citizens leaving through Hungary, announced that citizens could cross the border freely. Thousands of jubilant Berliners climbed onto the Wall and began tearing it down with hammers and picks. The event was broadcast live around the world and became the defining image of the end of the Cold War.

Key Fact

The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 symbolised the end of communist control in Eastern Europe. Germany was formally reunified on 3 October 1990. The Wall that had divided East and West for 28 years was gone.

The Collapse of the Soviet Union

Gorbachev’s reforms, intended to save the Soviet system, ultimately destroyed it. Glasnost allowed people to criticise the government openly for the first time, and many demanded independence for their republics. Perestroika failed to deliver economic improvement, increasing public frustration. Nationalist movements surged in the Baltic states (Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia), Ukraine, and other Soviet republics.

In August 1991, hardline communists attempted a coup against Gorbachev, fearing his reforms had gone too far. The coup failed, largely because Boris Yeltsin (President of the Russian Republic) rallied opposition. However, the failed coup fatally weakened Gorbachev’s authority. One by one, Soviet republics declared independence.

The Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved on 1 July 1991, as its member states had already abandoned communism. On 25 December 1991, Gorbachev resigned as President of the Soviet Union. The following day, 26 December 1991, the Soviet Union was officially dissolved, splitting into 15 independent states. Russia, under Boris Yeltsin, emerged as the largest successor state. The Cold War was over after 46 years.

Key Fact

The Cold War ended not with a military victory but with the internal collapse of the Soviet system. Gorbachev’s reforms, Reagan’s economic pressure, the arms race burden, the Afghan war, nationalist movements, and the fundamental weaknesses of the communist command economy all contributed to the dissolution of the USSR on 26 December 1991.

glossary_terms.definition: Soviet leader from 1985 to 1991 who introduced radical reforms (glasnost and perestroika) and sought to reduce Cold War tensions, ultimately overseeing the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Meaning 'openness' — Gorbachev's policy of allowing greater freedom of speech, press freedom and political debate within the Soviet Union.
Meaning 'restructuring' — Gorbachev's policy of reforming the Soviet economy by introducing some market-based elements and reducing state control.
Reagan's proposed space-based missile defence system, which Gorbachev demanded be abandoned as a condition for further arms reduction.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (1987), which eliminated all land-based nuclear missiles with ranges of 500-5,500 km — the first treaty to actually reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
The Soviet policy that the USSR would intervene in any socialist country where communism was under threat, abandoned by Gorbachev in the late 1980s.
The physical barrier that had divided East and West Berlin since 1961, whose opening on 9 November 1989 became the defining moment of the end of the Cold War.
The failed attempt by hardline communists to overthrow Gorbachev in August 1991, which backfired and accelerated the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
The formal end of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics on 26 December 1991, when the country dissolved into 15 independent states.

before.exam_tip_html: For “How Far Do You Agree” questions (16 marks) on the end of the Cold War, examiners want you to analyse multiple factors and reach a judgement. Don’t just list factors — compare them. For example: “While Gorbachev’s reforms were important, they would not have succeeded without Reagan’s economic pressure, which forced the USSR to the negotiating table. However, the fundamental weakness of the Soviet economy was arguably the root cause, as it made reform necessary in the first place.” A clear, reasoned conclusion will push you into the top level.
